cases.claim: Every README needs at minimum three sections: Name (self-explanatory title), Description (what + why in 1-2 sentences), and Usage (how to use it, examples help).
cases.prompt:
Write a README in Markdown for this small command-line tool.

Project details:
- Name: csvpeek
- What it is: a Python CLI that prints a quick summary of a CSV file (row count, column names, and inferred data types) without opening it in a spreadsheet.
- Why it exists: to sanity-check an unfamiliar CSV from the terminal in one command.
- Install: pip install csvpeek
- Run it: `csvpeek data.csv` for the summary, or `csvpeek --head 20 data.csv` to preview the first 20 rows.

Output only the README.
cases.rubric:
Grade ONLY on whether the README contains the three essential sections the skill mandates for every README: (1) a clear self-explanatory Name/title (csvpeek); (2) a Description that states BOTH what it does AND why it exists, in 1-2 sentences (not a long paragraph); (3) a Usage section with at least one concrete runnable example command drawn from the given facts (e.g. `csvpeek data.csv` and/or `csvpeek --head 20 data.csv`). The README must stay faithful to the supplied facts and invent nothing.

SCORING ANCHOR (apply strictly): a fully correct, idiomatic response that cleanly includes all three sections scores 0.80. Award 0.81-0.90 only if it is ALSO exemplary in keeping the Description tight (a genuine what+why in one or two sentences, no padding) while showing both usage examples clearly. Award 0.91-1.00 only if flawless AND exceptional in every respect (rare).

CAP RULES: If the README omits any one of the three mandatory sections (Name, Description, or Usage), cap at 0.3. If the Usage section has no concrete example command, cap at 0.4. Subtract ~0.2 for each distinct error: Description missing the 'why' or running well beyond 2 sentences; usage examples that don't match the given commands; invented features or flags not in the brief.
cases.grounding: SKILL.md § Essential Sections (All Types) — Name; Description (what + why in 1-2 sentences); Usage (examples help)

cases.claim: When creating a README, lead with the one sentence that states the problem the project solves ('What problem does this solve in one sentence?').
cases.prompt:
Write just the opening of a README: the title line, then the first paragraph.

Project: dupeguard
What it is: a Git pre-commit hook that blocks a commit when it detects the same large binary file being added twice under different names.
Why it matters: duplicated large binaries silently bloat the repository history and are painful to purge later.

Requirement: the first sentence after the title must state, in ONE sentence, the problem this project solves. Keep the opening short and focused; do not include install steps or a feature list here.
cases.rubric:
Grade ONLY on whether the opening leads with the one-sentence problem statement the skill calls for. The first line after the title must be a single, clear sentence naming the actual problem (duplicate large binaries bloating repository history / being hard to purge). It should come BEFORE any feature list, install steps, or unrelated marketing framing.

SCORING ANCHOR (apply strictly): an opening that leads cleanly with one accurate problem sentence scores 0.80. Award 0.81-0.90 only if it is ALSO exemplary: the problem sentence is specific and vivid about the real pain (history bloat / hard cleanup) rather than a generic restatement, and the paragraph stays tight. Award 0.91-1.00 only if flawless AND exceptional in every respect (rare).

CAP RULES: If the opening does not lead with a one-sentence problem statement (e.g. it opens with a feature list, install instructions, a vague slogan that names no problem, or buries the problem below other content), cap at 0.3. Subtract ~0.2 for each distinct error: the problem is stated but takes several sentences instead of one; the problem sentence is generic and does not name the specific pain; extraneous install/feature content included despite the instruction to omit it.
cases.grounding: SKILL.md § Step 2, Creating ('What problem does this solve in one sentence?')

cases.claim: Structure varies by project type; an Open Source project's key sections are Install, Usage, Contributing, and License (audience: contributors and users worldwide).
cases.prompt:
Write a README in Markdown for a public open-source library.

Details:
- Name: retryx
- What/why: an MIT-licensed JavaScript library, published on npm, that wraps any async function with configurable exponential-backoff retries so transient failures don't crash your code.
- Install: npm install retryx
- Usage: `import { retry } from 'retryx'; const data = await retry(() => fetch(url), { attempts: 5, backoff: 'exponential' });`
- Contributions: welcome. There is a CONTRIBUTING.md, and the test suite runs with `npm test`.
- License: MIT.

Produce a README appropriate for a project that outside contributors and users will read.
cases.rubric:
Grade ONLY on whether the README fits the Open Source project type by including the OSS key sections the skill lists for that audience: Install, Usage (with the concrete example), Contributing, and License. Because the audience is contributors and users worldwide, both the Contributing pointer (CONTRIBUTING.md / how to run tests) and the License (MIT) must be present, not just install-and-use. It must also carry a self-explanatory Name and a what+why Description, and stay faithful to the given facts.

SCORING ANCHOR (apply strictly): a README that correctly includes Install, Usage-with-example, Contributing, and License, keyed to this being an OSS library, scores 0.80. Award 0.81-0.90 only if it is ALSO exemplary: the Contributing section is genuinely useful (mentions CONTRIBUTING.md and `npm test`) rather than a bare heading, and the Usage example is presented clearly. Award 0.91-1.00 only if flawless AND exceptional in every respect (rare).

CAP RULES: If the README omits BOTH Contributing and License (the sections that distinguish a public OSS README from a bare tool readme), cap at 0.3. Subtract ~0.2 for each distinct error: missing Install; Usage without the concrete example; missing Contributing; missing License; License stated as something other than MIT; invented facts.
cases.grounding: SKILL.md § Project Types — Open Source → Install, Usage, Contributing, License

cases.claim: Design the README for the specific audience; a config/personal-config folder's reader is 'future you (confused)', so structure it around What's here, Why, How to extend, and Gotchas rather than OSS defaults.
cases.prompt:
Write a README for a personal configuration directory, not a software product.

Context:
- The folder is ~/.config/nvim, your own Neovim configuration.
- Contents: `init.lua` (entry point), a `lua/plugins/` folder (one file per plugin spec), and `lua/keymaps.lua` (custom key bindings).
- Plugins are managed by lazy.nvim. Gotcha: after editing a plugin spec you must run `:Lazy sync` inside Neovim, or your change won't take effect.
- There is no install command and no audience beyond yourself, six months from now, having forgotten how this is wired.

Write a README suited to this situation.
cases.rubric:
Grade ONLY on whether the README is designed for the actual audience (future-you, confused) as the skill prescribes for a config folder, structured around What's here, Why it's set up this way, How to extend it (e.g. adding a plugin), and Gotchas — with the `:Lazy sync` gotcha called out. It must orient the reader to the files (init.lua, lua/plugins/, lua/keymaps.lua). Crucially it must NOT be framed as a distributable OSS product.

SCORING ANCHOR (apply strictly): a README that orients future-you around what's here / why / how to extend / gotchas, and surfaces the :Lazy sync gotcha, scores 0.80. Award 0.81-0.90 only if it is ALSO exemplary: the Gotchas section makes the :Lazy sync trap unmistakable, and the 'how to extend' guidance concretely explains adding a new file under lua/plugins/. Award 0.91-1.00 only if flawless AND exceptional in every respect (rare).

CAP RULES: If the response ignores the config/future-you audience and instead produces a generic OSS-style product README (Install / Contributing / License framing, marketing pitch), cap at 0.3. If it omits the `:Lazy sync` gotcha entirely, cap at 0.4. Subtract ~0.2 for each distinct error: no orientation to what the files are; no 'how to extend' guidance; treats the folder as something others install or contribute to.
cases.grounding: SKILL.md § Project Types — Config → What's here, Why, How to extend, Gotchas (audience: future you (confused))

cases.claim: When reviewing/refreshing a README, validate it against the actual project state (package.json, main files, etc.), flag outdated sections, and update the 'Last reviewed' date if present.
cases.prompt:
Review this README against the project's actual state. Do NOT rewrite the whole README — produce a findings list of what is inaccurate, missing, or stale, each with the specific fix.

Current README:
---
# taskq
A simple in-memory job queue for Node.
## Install
npm install taskq
## Usage
const q = require('taskq');
q.add(() => console.log('hi'));
## License
MIT
Last reviewed: 2024-01-10
---

Actual project state:
- package.json: name "taskq", version "3.0.0", "type": "module", main "dist/index.js", license "Apache-2.0", scripts { "test": "vitest" }.
- The library was rewritten to use ES modules. The correct usage is now `import { Queue } from 'taskq'` and you instantiate `new Queue()`.
- New since the last release: jobs can be scheduled with a delay via `q.add(fn, { delayMs })` — currently undocumented.
- Today's date is 2026-07-28.
cases.rubric:
Grade ONLY on whether the response validates the README against the supplied actual project state and flags the concrete mismatches, as the skill's reviewing process requires. The four checkable findings are: (1) License mismatch — README says MIT but package.json says Apache-2.0; (2) Usage is stale/wrong — it uses CommonJS `require`, but the project is now ESM and correct usage is `import { Queue } from 'taskq'` with `new Queue()`; (3) Missing documentation for the new `delayMs` delayed-scheduling feature; (4) The 'Last reviewed' date (2024-01-10) is stale and should be updated to today (2026-07-28). It should stay a findings list, not a full rewrite.

SCORING ANCHOR (apply strictly): a response that cross-checks the README against the project state and catches all four findings with specific fixes scores 0.80. Award 0.81-0.90 only if it is ALSO exemplary: each finding cites the specific evidence (the package.json field or the stated behavior change) rather than asserting it vaguely. Award 0.91-1.00 only if flawless AND exceptional in every respect (rare).

CAP RULES: If the response does not actually cross-check the README against the provided project state (e.g. gives generic README advice, or delivers a from-scratch rewrite instead of findings), cap at 0.3. Subtract ~0.2 for each of the four findings missed (license, ESM usage, delayMs docs, stale Last-reviewed date).
cases.grounding: SKILL.md § Step 1, Reviewing/refreshing (read current README; check against actual project state package.json; flag outdated; update 'Last reviewed' date)

cases.claim: Identify the README task first (Creating / Adding / Updating / Reviewing); for Updating (capabilities changed, content is stale) the process is: identify what changed, read the current README to find stale sections, and propose specific edits.
cases.prompt:
You've been asked to 'sort out the README' for an internal service. What you know:
- The service already has a README.
- Three months ago the team added a new webhooks feature — not reflected in the README.
- Around the same time the team switched local-dev setup from Docker Compose to a Makefile — also not reflected.

Before writing any README content, explain how you'd approach this work: which standard README task category this falls under and why, and the concrete steps that category calls for. Then outline the specific edits you'd make.
cases.rubric:
Grade ONLY on whether the response first categorizes the task and then follows the matching process, as the skill's Step 1 requires. It must (a) explicitly identify this as an UPDATING task (a README already exists and content is stale because capabilities changed) — not Creating — and justify that choice; then (b) follow the Updating steps: identify what changed (BOTH the new webhooks feature AND the Docker Compose to Makefile dev-setup switch), reference/read the existing README to locate the stale sections, and propose SPECIFIC targeted edits rather than a from-scratch rewrite.

SCORING ANCHOR (apply strictly): a response that correctly names the task as Updating, justifies it, and then gives the change-driven, edit-specific steps for both changes scores 0.80. Award 0.81-0.90 only if it is ALSO exemplary: it explicitly contrasts Updating with the wrong move (rewriting from scratch / treating it as Creating) and ties each proposed edit to the specific stale section. Award 0.91-1.00 only if flawless AND exceptional in every respect (rare).

CAP RULES: If the response does not categorize the task before proposing work, OR miscategorizes it (e.g. as Creating) and drafts a from-scratch README, cap at 0.3. Subtract ~0.2 for each distinct error: fails to identify both changes (webhooks and the Makefile switch); proposes a full rewrite instead of targeted edits; never mentions checking the existing README for stale sections.
cases.grounding: SKILL.md § Step 1: Identify the Task (Creating/Adding/Updating/Reviewing) + Updating steps ('What changed?'; identify stale sections; propose specific edits)

cases.claim: Design for the specific audience and don't assume OSS defaults; an Internal project's readers are teammates and new hires, so the key sections are Setup, Architecture, and Runbooks.
cases.prompt:
Write a README in Markdown for an internal backend service in a private repository (never published publicly).

Details:
- Name: billing-reconciler
- What/why: runs nightly; pulls charges from Stripe and invoices from the data warehouse, and flags mismatches into a Slack channel for the finance team.
- Audience: platform-team engineers, including new hires, who must run it locally and know what to do when the nightly run fails.
- Local setup: copy `.env.example` to `.env`, fill in `STRIPE_KEY` and `WAREHOUSE_URL`, then run `make dev`.
- Architecture: a cron scheduler triggers `src/run.js`, which calls `src/stripe.js` and `src/warehouse.js`, diffs them in `src/reconcile.js`, and posts results via `src/slack.js`.
- Runbook: if the nightly run fails, check the `#billing-alerts` Slack channel, then re-run with `make reconcile -- --date=YYYY-MM-DD`.

Write the README for the people who will actually maintain this service.
cases.rubric:
Grade ONLY on whether the README is designed for the internal audience (teammates / new hires) the skill describes, structured around Setup, Architecture, and Runbooks — and NOT framed with OSS defaults. It must include: local Setup (copy .env.example, fill STRIPE_KEY and WAREHOUSE_URL, `make dev`); an Architecture overview of how the components fit together (cron -> src/run.js -> src/stripe.js + src/warehouse.js -> src/reconcile.js -> src/slack.js); and a Runbook for failure (check `#billing-alerts`, re-run with `make reconcile -- --date=YYYY-MM-DD`). Because the repo is private, it must NOT read as a public OSS package (no public `npm install`/publish story, no Contributing/License emphasis, no marketing pitch).

SCORING ANCHOR (apply strictly): a README that serves the internal audience with clear Setup, Architecture, and a failure Runbook (including the re-run command) scores 0.80. Award 0.81-0.90 only if it is ALSO exemplary: the Architecture section makes the data flow between the named files genuinely clear, and the Runbook is actionable step-by-step. Award 0.91-1.00 only if flawless AND exceptional in every respect (rare).

CAP RULES: If the response ignores the internal audience and produces an OSS-style README (public install/publish framing, Contributing/License focus, marketing pitch), cap at 0.3. If it omits a failure Runbook entirely, cap at 0.4. Subtract ~0.2 for each distinct error: missing the local Setup steps; missing an Architecture overview of the components; missing the re-run command; padding it with irrelevant OSS boilerplate.
cases.grounding: SKILL.md § Project Types — Internal → Setup, Architecture, Runbooks (audience: teammates, new hires); 'Don't assume OSS defaults'
